title: SAE Toolkit
text: This SAE toolkit shows how to adapt the tutorial workflow to your own survey, geography, and outcome by mapping your data to a common schema and apply reusable scripts.

2. Prepare the input tables
The workflow expects a set of datasets, linked by area_id and time_id values, with unit_id as the survey respondent identifier.

Domain frame
One row for every area-time cell that should receive an estimate. This table defines the target grid, including cells with no survey respondents.



Column
Meaning




area_id
Area to estimate


time_id
Time period to estimate

Optional area or period labels





Survey indicator
One row per respondent-period for the outcome being estimated, together with the unit-level predictors.



Column
Meaning




unit_id
Respondent identifier


area_id
Area assigned to the respondent


time_id
Survey period


indicator
Outcome used in estimation (binary or continuous)


weight
Survey design weight


strata
Survey stratum, if available


predictors
Unit predictors (age, sex, car ownership, etc.)





Area predictors
One row per area, with predictors used to explain spatial differences in the outcome. These are used in area-level SAE and can also support unit-level SAE, when they provide the area-level summaries to aggregate predictions.



Column
Meaning




area_id
Area identifier


cov_*
Predictors (transformed) for modelling


raw_*
Predictors (original) for interpretation and aggregation





Poststratification table
Used when model predictions are aggregated over population groups to produce the final estimate in the Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP) workflow.







Column
Meaning




area_id
Area identifier


time_id
Time period


population groups
Age, sex, household type, or other poststratification categories


pop_count
Population count for each cell

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.


max_variance <- max(
  direct_walk$variance[direct_walk$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

direct_walk_model <- direct_walk |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(.data$direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(.data$variance) ~ max_variance,
      .data$variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$variance
    )
  )

INLA uses numeric indices to encode space and time, so we create time_inla_id and area_inla_id to index survey years and MSOAs. We also provide an adjacency graph for the structured spatial effect. Here, we use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels),
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(.data$area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)


Finally, we assemble the modelling data for INLA by comining the direct estimates with the area predictors and the numeric indices for the temporal and spatial effects.

model_data <- direct_walk_model |>
  left_join(area_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  arrange(.data$time_id, .data$area_inla_id)

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Temporal
M0 plus temporal random walk


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and no-car households


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+Spatial
M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency



The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.







Temporal model
Description




rw1
First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods.


rw2
Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series.


ar1
Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years.










Spatial model
Description




besag
Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation.


bym2
Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, phi, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured.



With only three survey years, rw1 is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, bym2 is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When fitting area-level FH models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
scale passes the inverse sampling variance to INLA, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
control.family fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit in case of multiple specifications.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we use WAIC or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.


Code
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
3 Report estimates and uncertainty
To extract the estimates for this model, we take the fitted-value summary from the INLA object and bind it back to the area-time rows used in the model fit. For transparency, the output also retains the direct estimates, sample sizes, and direct-estimate variances. The final model estimates are reported with uncertainty, shown here using the width of the posterior 95% credible interval.

model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id, msoa_name, direct_estimate, variance, n)

fitted_values <- fh_fits[["M4 +Spatial"]]$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble()

final_fh_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    msoa_name,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    n,
    fh_estimate = mean,
    fh_variance = sd^2,
    fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
    fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
    fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower,
    fh_std_resid = (direct_estimate - fh_estimate) /  sqrt(variance + fh_variance)
  )

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
4 Further diagnostics
To better understand how the FH results are produced, we can inspect the contribution of each of the model components. The diagnostics below examine how estimates change as predictors, spatial structure, and temporal structure are added, and then review uncertainty and hyperparameters to understand where the model is borrowing strength most strongly.


Code
model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    msoa_name,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    n
  )

fh_results <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    bind_cols(
      model_output_frame,
      as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)
    ) |>
      transmute(
        model = model_name,
        area_id,
        time_id,
        msoa_name,
        direct_estimate,
        variance,
        n,
        fh_estimate = mean,
        fh_variance = sd^2,
        fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
        fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
        fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower,
        fh_std_resid = (direct_estimate - fh_estimate) /  sqrt(variance + fh_variance)
      )
  }
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(model_formulas)))



4.1 Direct To Baseline Model
We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure to understand how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates.


Code
fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per area-time cell, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]] - .data$variance
  )

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$time_id))







Area-time cells with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M0 pulls them more strongly toward its baseline prediction. The Bayesian FH fit also produces posterior estimates for cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance, allowing sparse or unsampled area-time cells to remain in the output with explicit uncertainty.

4.2 Adding Predictors
After the WAIC comparison, we inspect local estimate changes to see where the model moves the target estimates and whether those movements are substantively plausible. In Fay-Herriot SAE, adding predictors changes the expected value for each area-time cell, and unstable direct estimates are pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions when the predictors are relevant.
For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).







Code
m2_to_m3_drivers <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    work_from_home = cov_share_work_from_home,
    students = cov_share_students,
    routine_semiroutine = cov_share_routine_semiroutine
  ) |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(
    change_group = case_when(
      estimate_change >= quantile(estimate_change, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Raised most with M3",
      estimate_change <= quantile(estimate_change, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Lowered most with M3",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

m2_to_m3_drivers |>
  drop_na(change_group) |>
  group_by(.data$change_group) |>
  summarise(
    `Work from home` = mean(.data$work_from_home, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Students` = mean(.data$students, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Routine or semi-routine` = mean(.data$routine_semiroutine, na.rm = TRUE),

4.3 Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be examined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher tau means the random effect varies less.
phi is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of 0.5 means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.

The temporal effect has a high tau than the spatial effect, indicating smaller differences between survey waves than between MSOAs. Meanwhile, the low spatial phi (less than 0.5) indicates that only a small share of the remaining between-area variation follows the spatial weights; most of it remains unstructured. We can see where that structured spatial component affects the estimates by mapping the change from M3 to M4. In most areas the changes are small, with some clustered adjustments where neighbouring MSOAs share similar estimated walking rates, such as the more urban southern region.





In practice, the decision to pick the right SAE model specification should be assessed holistically using model diagnostics, stepwise changes across models, and domain knowledge. These checks help decide whether it should be further enriched with additional predictors, or alternative spatial or temporal structures.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text: This workbook introduces the survey source, defines the estimand, documents the synthetic geography, and explains the analysis-ready datasets used by the estimation workflows that follow.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the three survey waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW) in 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are originally geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. Possible to demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



From here on, the survey period labels are simplified to their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as and referred to as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow

2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. In this worked example, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.

title: Bayesian Battese-Harter-Fuller Unit-Level Model
text:
1 Prepare model and aggregation data
Before preparing the model inputs, we create consistent numeric indices for each area and survey year so that INLA can attach random effects to the correct area and period, as well as a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph .adj as input, similar to what we did in the previous FH model workbook.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(.data$area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

model_data contains the sampled respondent records used to fit the model.

title: Bayesian Battese-Harter-Fuller Unit-Level Model
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit linear mixed models to respondent-level records, then use them to predict area-time means. Because the response variable is binary, the fitted values are interpreted as predicted probabilities.
We specify two unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
Temporal + spatial
Respondent outcome with a temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+No-car
M1 plus respondent-level no-car access




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  no_car +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 Temporal + Spatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +No-car" = m2_formula
)

Conceptually, the workflow has two steps: fit the respondent-level model, then evaluate it for each area-time. We implement this by binding the observed respondent rows and the area-time aggregation rows into a single input table before fitting. The area-time rows to have their estimates predicted have indicator = NA, signalling to INLA to return fitted values for them.

model_agg_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "model",
      indicator,
      no_car,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    ),
  aggregation_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "aggregation",
      indicator = NA_real_,
      no_car,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    )
)

fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_agg_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)







Note



When fitting unit-level BHF models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) ensures that fitted values are returned for the full input table, so the predictions for the aggregation rows can be extracted after fitting.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit across candidate specifications.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we again use WAIC as a first check. WAIC is a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity. Here, the lower WAIC for M2 shows that adding the no-car predictor improves the model predictive power as expected.

text:
3 Report estimates and uncertainty
Using M2 as the selected model, we extract predictions for the target area-time rows, marked in the INLA input as row_type == "aggregation". We then report the posterior mean as the final estimate and use the lower and upper bounds of the 95% credible interval to describe uncertainty.

  slice(which(model_agg_data$row_type == "aggregation"))

  aggregation_data |> select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id),
  bhf_m2_fitted_values

    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    bhf_estimate = pmin(pmax(mean, 0), 1),
    bhf_variance = sd^2,

This simple BHF example is fitted to unweighted respondent records and uses only one respondent-level predictor. title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often want to use survey data at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. This may involve comparing places, monitoring change over time, identifying local inequalities, or linking survey outcomes to area-level conditions. The problem is that most surveys are not designed to support reliable estimates at all geographic levels and time periods. When responses are broken down by area and year, some cells have only a few respondents and others have none.
This tutorial presents a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small-area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics. It focuses on method choice and shows how these approaches can be implemented in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference is used to combine survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. One advantage is that uncertainty of a modelled estimate is returned as posterior distributions for each estimate, which faciliates interpretation in policy contexts.
For code implementation, the examples are fitted with R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Tutorial structure

The tutorial is selective. It covers the SAE methods most relevant to common Urban Analytics survey and auxiliary datasets, with the choice driven by outcome type, available survey information, auxiliary data, and population structure.


Estimation setup
Start by specifying the estimand: outcome, target population, areas, and time periods. This defines the area-time cells that need estimates and the inputs required for each possible route.
Direct estimation
Compute survey design-based estimates and sampling variances for observed area-time cells. If these estimates are precise enough and have adequate coverage, direct estimation may be sufficient.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Use this route when direct estimates exist but are too noisy or incomplete, and the available auxiliary data are area-level predictors. The model smooths direct estimates across predictors, neighbouring areas, and time periods.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model
Use this route when survey microdata are available and the outcome can be modelled at respondent or household level. The fitted unit-level relationship is then aggregated to area-time estimates using area-level summaries of the predictors.
Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP)
Use this route when population counts are available for poststratification cells, such as area by age by sex. The model predicts outcomes for each population cell and weights those predictions back to area-time estimates.




Tutorial data

The tutorial uses synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales.
The maps and estimates illustrate the workflow and should not be interpreted as empirical findings for specific places in Wales. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup step.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.

Direct estimation is the starting point for the SAE workflow. At this stage, each area-time estimate, or an MSOA-year cell in this example, is calculated only from the survey respondents observed in that area and wave, using the matched survey weight. This gives us a transparent baseline before any model-based smoothing is introduced and shows where direct estimates are unstable, missing, or based on very small samples, helping us decide whether model-based small area estimation is needed.

title: Direct Estimation
text:
2 Calculate direct estimates
We use svyby() from the survey package to compute the weighted share and its uncertainty diagnostics for every area-time cell with usable observations. It then completes the area-by-time grid so missing cells are retained for modelling.

# Define survey design
walk_design <- svydesign(
  ids = as.formula("~1"),
  strata = as.formula("~strata"),
  weights = as.formula("~weight"),
  data = survey_walk
)

# Calculate direct estimate and uncertainty
direct_walk_estimates <- svyby(
  formula = as.formula("~indicator"),
  by = as.formula("~area_id + time_id"),
  design = walk_design,
  FUN = svymean,
  vartype = "se",
  na.rm = TRUE,
  keep.names = FALSE
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_estimate = .data$indicator,
    variance = .data$se^2
  )

# Calculate sample size per area-time cell
direct_walk_counts <- survey_walk |>
  group_by(across(all_of(c("area_id", "time_id")))) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Join
direct_walk <- domain_frame |>
  left_join(direct_walk_estimates, by = c(
    "area_id", "time_id"
  )) |>
  left_join(direct_walk_counts, by = c(
    "area_id", "time_id"
  )) |>
  mutate(n = replace_na(.data$n, 0L))

title: Direct Estimation
text:
3 Assess precision and coverage
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because it makes three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and MSOAs, leaving some area-time cells with much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimates over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves, which may reflect real behavioural change or sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, small samples can contain only one response value, producing zero or unrealistically low variances.

direct_summary_by_wave <- direct_walk |>
  group_by(.data$time_id) |>
  summarise(
    `Usable observations` = sum(.data$n),
    `MSOAs without direct estimates` = sum(is.na(.data$direct_estimate)),
    `MSOAs with zero variance` = sum(.data$variance == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median sample size` = median(.data$n),
    `Median direct estimate` = round(
      median(.data$direct_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
      3
    ),
    `Median variance` = round(
      median(.data$variance, na.rm = TRUE),

Code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(.data$area_id, "W"))
The BHF workbook ended by pointing to the next limitation of unit-level SAE: once the model uses predictors such as age and sex, aggregation should use population counts for those predictor cells rather than a single area-level average. Here we use MRP in two stages. First, we fit a respondent-level model and poststratify over the observed age-sex population cells. Then we smooth those age-sex adjusted MSOA-year estimates with an area-level no-car household covariate and spatio-temporal random effects.

title: SAE with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
1 Prepare modelling and poststratification data
As in previous workbooks, we first create consistent numeric indices for each MSOA and survey year, and a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph for the spatial effect.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(.data$area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

The MRP workflow needs two inputs:

model_data, the sampled respondent records used to fit the model;
poststrat_data, the population cells over which predictions are averaged.


1.1 Respondent model data
The survey file contains respondent-level age, sex, and walking outcome fields.
It is essential for the unit-level predictors to be identical to the ones present in the poststratification table. Therefore, age is grouped into the same five-year bands and sex is also recoded as Male and Female. The respondent-level no-car indicator is deliberately left out of this model, because we do not have reliable population counts for no-car status within each age-sex cell.

title: SAE with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We first fit binomial unit-level models for the age-sex poststratification step. The outcome is the respondent walking indicator, and predictions for the poststratification rows are returned on the probability scale.



Model
Name
Specification




M0
Baseline
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M1
+Age
M0 plus age band


M2
+Sex
M1 plus sex




m0_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m1_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Age" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Sex" = m2_formula
)

The observed respondent rows and the poststratification rows are combined before fitting. Rows with indicator = NA are not used in the likelihood, but INLA still returns their fitted values, which are needed for poststratification.

model_poststrat_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "model",
      indicator,
      trials = 1L,
      age_band,
      sex,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    ),
  poststrat_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "poststrat",
      indicator = NA_real_,
      trials = 1L,
      age_band,
      sex,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    )
)

fit_mrp_model <- function(formula, config = FALSE) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = model_poststrat_data$trials,
    data = model_poststrat_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = config)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- imap(
  model_formulas,
  \(formula, model_name) {
    fit_mrp_model(
      formula = formula,
      config = identical(model_name, "M2 +Sex")
    )
  }
)

We use WAIC as an initial model check. Lower WAIC indicates better expected predictive fit after penalising model complexity.

These maps should be read together. The estimate row shows the age-sex poststratified and smoothed spatial pattern, the uncertainty row shows where the model remains less precise, and the residual row flags places where the weighted direct estimate is far from the MRP estimate after accounting for both sources of uncertainty.

5.1 Comparison diagnostics
The first comparison checks whether MRP agrees with the previous direct, BHF, and Fay–Herriot estimates. Points far from the equality line are the cells to inspect first, especially when the direct-estimate sample size is large.





The second comparison maps the MRP shift from BHF and the change in credible-interval width. This is the most direct diagnostic for the poststratification and smoothing steps: large spatial shifts indicate where age-sex composition and the area-level no-car covariate move the estimate, while positive uncertainty gains indicate cells where MRP is more precise than the BHF output.





The final MRP output should be used when the age-sex population adjustment is part of the estimand. The BHF estimates remain useful as a unit-level benchmark, while the direct estimates remain the main check on whether modelled values are drifting away from the survey evidence.

title: SAE with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
3 Age-sex poststratification
For MRP, uncertainty should be aggregated after poststratification rather than by averaging cell-level standard errors. We sample from the joint posterior of the age-sex model’s linear predictors, transform each draw to probabilities, and then poststratify each draw over the age-sex population cells. The resulting area-time posterior samples give the age-sex adjusted estimate and variance used by the smoothing stage.


Code
mrp_age_sex_fit <- mrp_fits[["M2 +Sex"]]
poststrat_rows <- which(model_poststrat_data$row_type == "poststrat")
n_posterior_samples <- 300L

set.seed(20260706)
mrp_posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = n_posterior_samples,
  result = mrp_age_sex_fit
)

extract_poststrat_probabilities <- function(sample, poststrat_rows) {
  latent <- sample$latent
  predictor_index <- grep("^Predictor", rownames(latent))

  if (length(predictor_index) < max(poststrat_rows)) {
    stop("Posterior sample does not contain all fitted predictor rows.")
  }

  predictor_values <- as.numeric(latent[predictor_index, 1])
  plogis(predictor_values[poststrat_rows])
}

cell_probability_samples <- vapply(
  mrp_posterior_samples,
  extract_poststrat_probabilities,
  numeric(length(poststrat_rows)),
  poststrat_rows = poststrat_rows
)

area_time_key <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")
weighted_cell_samples <- cell_probability_samples * poststrat_data$pop_count
sample_numerators <- rowsum(weighted_cell_samples, group = area_time_key, reorder = FALSE)
sample_denominators <- rowsum(poststrat_data$pop_count, group = area_time_key, reorder = FALSE)
area_time_samples <- sweep(sample_numerators, 1, as.numeric(sample_denominators), "/")

mrp_sample_summary <- tibble(
  area_time_key = rownames(area_time_samples),
  age_sex_mrp_estimate = rowMeans(area_time_samples),
  age_sex_mrp_variance = apply(area_time_samples, 1, var),
  age_sex_mrp_lower = apply(area_time_samples, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
  age_sex_mrp_upper = apply(area_time_samples, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
) |>
  mutate(
    age_sex_mrp_ci_width = .data$age_sex_mrp_upper - .data$age_sex_mrp_lower
  ) |>
  separate(
    area_time_key,
    into = c("area_id", "time_id"),
    sep = "__",
    convert = TRUE
  )

mrp_age_sex_results <- domain_frame |>
  select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id) |>
  left_join(mrp_sample_summary, by = c("area_id", "time_id"))

title: SAE with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
4 Smooth poststratified estimates
The second stage treats the age-sex poststratified estimates as area-time observations with known uncertainty. The MSOA no-car household share enters here as an area-level predictor, alongside temporal and spatial smoothing.

positive_mrp_variance <- mrp_age_sex_results$age_sex_mrp_variance[
  mrp_age_sex_results$age_sex_mrp_variance > 0
]

max_mrp_variance <- max(positive_mrp_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

if (!is.finite(max_mrp_variance)) {
  max_mrp_variance <- 1
}

smoothing_data <- mrp_age_sex_results |>
  left_join(area_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(.data$age_sex_mrp_estimate) ~ max_mrp_variance,
      is.na(.data$age_sex_mrp_variance) ~ max_mrp_variance,
      .data$age_sex_mrp_variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_mrp_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$age_sex_mrp_variance
    )
  ) |>
  drop_na(no_car_share_scaled, time_inla_id, area_inla_id)

smooth_formula <- age_sex_mrp_estimate ~
  no_car_share_scaled +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

mrp_smoother_fit <- inla(
  formula = smooth_formula,
  family = "gaussian",
  data = smoothing_data,
  scale = 1 / smoothing_data$adj_variance,
  control.family = list(
    hyper = list(
      prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
    )
  ),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
)

smoother_fitted_values <- mrp_smoother_fit$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble()

mrp_m2_results <- bind_cols(
  smoothing_data |>
    select(
      area_id,
      msoa_name,
      time_id,
      no_car_share,
      no_car_share_scaled,
      age_sex_mrp_estimate,
      age_sex_mrp_variance,
      age_sex_mrp_ci_width
    ),
  smoother_fitted_values
) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    no_car_share,
    no_car_share_scaled,
    age_sex_mrp_estimate,
    age_sex_mrp_variance,
    age_sex_mrp_ci_width,
    mrp_estimate = mean,
    mrp_variance = sd^2,
    mrp_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
    mrp_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
    mrp_ci_width = .data$mrp_upper - .data$mrp_lower
  )
